source_evidence.observation: The paper fixes A in R^(m x n), with m >= n and rank(A) = n, writes A = (a_1,...,a_n), and gives the exact-arithmetic baseline A = QR with Q^T Q = I_n and upper-triangular nonsingular R (PDF p. 2, printed p. 300, anchor: standing rectangular full-rank setup and equation (1)).

The standard Algorithm 1 computes r_kk = ||v_k||_2, whereas the paper says the required change is a Cholesky-like diagonal formula and names the resulting method Algorithm 2, CGS-P (PDF p. 2, printed p. 300, anchor: paragraph following Algorithm 1).

Algorithm 2 initializes r_11 = ||a_1||_2 and q_1 = a_1/r_11; for k = 2,...,n it computes s_k = Q_(k-1)^T a_k, v_k = a_k - Q_(k-1)s_k, psi_k = ||a_k||_2, phi_k = ||s_k||_2, r_kk = sqrt(psi_k-phi_k)sqrt(psi_k+phi_k), q_k = v_k/r_kk, and then assembles Q_k and R_k (PDF p. 3, printed p. 301, anchor: Algorithm 2).

The paper assumes IEEE floating-point arithmetic and states fl(x+y) = (x+y)(1+delta), |delta| <= epsilon_M, for results in the normalized range; it also uses (1+epsilon_M)^(p(n)) = 1+p(n)epsilon_M+O(epsilon_M^2) for modest p(n), treating the quadratic term as insignificant (PDF p. 3, printed p. 301, anchor: paragraphs following Algorithm 2).

The paper defines c_1 through c_4 and kappa_2(R_k), assumes c_4(m,k)epsilon_M kappa_2(R_k)^2 < 1 for every k, and states all five conclusions (4)-(8) for every k = 1,...,n, globally 'to within terms of O(epsilon_M^2)' (PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: equation (2) and Theorem 1).

The selected conclusion is ||I-Q_k^T Q_k||_2 <= c_4(m,k)kappa_2(R_k)^2 epsilon_M for each partial computed factor Q_k, under the theorem's global first-order convention (PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: Theorem 1, equation (7)).

The paper warns that when A does not satisfy Theorem 1's assumptions, phi_k >= psi_k can occur and Algorithm 2 can break down, producing Q and R that are not real matrices (PDF p. 7, printed p. 305, anchor: Remark 2).

The proof treats psi_k and phi_k as computed norms, states relative first-order bounds for them, and says that (3) yields nonsingular R and r_kk > 0, which in Algorithm 2 requires psi_k > phi_k (PDF p. 9, printed p. 307, anchor: Lemma 2 proof following equations (14)-(15)).

The proof uses Q_k = (A_k+Delta A_k)R_k^(-1) and expands I-Q_k^TQ_k as R_k^(-T)(E_k-A_k^T Delta A_k-(Delta A_k)^T A_k-(Delta A_k)^T Delta A_k)R_k^(-1); applying (4) and (5) gives c_4 = c_2+2c_1 and an explicit O(epsilon_M^2) remainder (PDF p. 14, printed p. 312, anchor: proof beginning 'To get (7)').

The proof derives ||Q_k||_2^2 <= 1+||I-Q_k^TQ_k||_2 <= 2+O(epsilon_M^2) from (7) and condition (3), and then takes square roots to obtain (8) (PDF p. 15, printed p. 313, anchor: paragraph beginning 'Finally, to get (8)').

binders: Inherited binders are matrix dimensions m,n and A in R^(m x n), with m >= n and rank(A) = n (PDF p. 2, printed p. 300, anchor: standing rectangular full-rank setup).

For each k in {1,...,n}, A_k in R^(m x k) is the matrix of the first k columns of A, while Q_k and R_k are the corresponding partial computed factors from the column-by-column algorithm (PDF p. 3, printed p. 301, anchor: Algorithm 2; PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: definition preceding Theorem 1).
epsilon_M denotes the machine unit of the floating-point arithmetic (PDF p. 3, printed p. 301, anchor: floating-point model; PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: Theorem 1).

The premise is quantified over every k = 1,...,n, and, under that premise, conclusions (4)-(8) are likewise asserted for every k = 1,...,n (PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: Theorem 1 and equation (3)).

Delta A_k and E_k are residual matrices introduced by equations (4) and (5), and mu_k is the scalar perturbation introduced by equation (6) (PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: Theorem 1, equations (4)-(6)).
hypotheses: The standing input assumption is A in R^(m x n), m >= n, with full column rank rank(A) = n; this is inherited rather than repeated inside Theorem 1 (PDF p. 2, printed p. 300, anchor: standing rectangular full-rank setup).

Q and R are the computed results of Algorithm 2, the Cholesky-like classical Gram-Schmidt algorithm CGS-P, in floating-point arithmetic with machine unit epsilon_M (PDF p. 3, printed p. 301, anchor: Algorithm 2; PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: opening sentence of Theorem 1).
For every k = 1,...,n, c_4(m,k)epsilon_M kappa_2(R_k)^2 < 1 (PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: Theorem 1, equation (3)).

The standing arithmetic model applies the stated relative-error formula to results in the normalized range and adopts a first-order approximation that neglects O(epsilon_M^2) contributions (PDF p. 3, printed p. 301, anchor: floating-point model and linear approximation).
conclusions: Equation (4): Delta A_k is defined by Q_k R_k - A_k = Delta A_k, and ||Delta A_k||_2 <= c_1(m,k)||A_k||_2 epsilon_M, under the global omission of O(epsilon_M^2) terms (PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: Theorem 1, equation (4)).

Equation (5): E_k is defined by R_k^T R_k - A_k^T A_k = E_k, and ||E_k||_2 <= c_2(m,k)||A_k||_2^2 epsilon_M, under the global omission of O(epsilon_M^2) terms (PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: Theorem 1, equation (5)).
Equation (6): ||R_k||_2 = ||A_k||_2(1+mu_k), with |mu_k| <= c_3(m,k)epsilon_M, under the global omission of O(epsilon_M^2) terms (PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: Theorem 1, equation (6)).

Equation (7), the selected result: ||I_k-Q_k^TQ_k||_2 <= c_4(m,k)kappa_2(R_k)^2 epsilon_M, under the global omission of O(epsilon_M^2) terms; I_k is the dimensionally required k x k identity (PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: Theorem 1, equation (7)).

Equation (8): ||Q_k||_2 <= sqrt(2), under the global omission of O(epsilon_M^2) terms (PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: Theorem 1, equation (8); PDF p. 15, printed p. 313, anchor: proof of equation (8)).
definitions_and_conventions: A = (a_1,...,a_n), Q = (q_1,...,q_n), and R = (r_jk); the algorithm constructs Q_k and R_k column by column (PDF p. 2, printed p. 300, anchor: notational conventions and Algorithm 1 setup; PDF p. 3, printed p. 301, anchor: Algorithm 2).
A_k is the first k columns of A (PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: definition immediately preceding Theorem 1).
c_1(m,1) = 1, while c_1(m,k) = 2*sqrt(2)*m*k + 2*sqrt(k) for k = 2,...,n (PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: equation (2), definition of c_1).
c_2(m,1) = m+2, while c_2(m,k) = 3.5*m*k^2 - 1.5*m*k + 16*k for k = 2,...,n (PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: equation (2), definition of c_2).
c_3(m,k) = 0.5*c_2(m,k), and c_4(m,k) = c_2(m,k)+2*c_1(m,k) (PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: equation (2), definitions of c_3 and c_4).
kappa_2(R_k) = ||R_k||_2 ||R_k^(-1)||_2 (PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: definition immediately preceding Theorem 1).

The identity in equation (7) is printed as I without a subscript; because Q_k is m x k, Q_k^TQ_k is k x k, so the dimensionally forced reading is I_k (PDF p. 3, printed p. 301, anchor: Algorithm 2 block dimensions; PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: equation (7)).
implicit_context: Theorem 1 inherits the paper's full-column-rank rectangular setup; it does not introduce a new arbitrary A independently of that setup (PDF p. 2, printed p. 300, anchor: standing setup; PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: Theorem 1).

The exact-arithmetic relation A = QR with Q^TQ = I_n is background only; Theorem 1 concerns computed Q_k and R_k and bounds their residuals and loss of orthogonality rather than asserting exact computed orthogonality (PDF p. 2, printed p. 300, anchor: equation (1); PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: equations (4)-(8)).

The paper says restriction (3) assures nonsingularity of R and is specifically what supports (7) and (8); it says a weaker assumption could yield bounds similar to (4)-(6) (PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: paragraph following Theorem 1).

The premise and selected conclusion use the condition number of each computed R_k, not kappa_2(A_k); Remark 1 only discusses how a variation may be related to kappa_2(A_k) (PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: Remark 1).

The proof of (7) is coupled to both residual conclusions (4) and (5): it substitutes Q_k = (A_k+Delta A_k)R_k^(-1), expands the exact defect identity, and bounds the linear residual terms by c_2+2c_1 while absorbing the quadratic Delta A_k term into O(epsilon_M^2) (PDF p. 14, printed p. 312, anchor: proof of equation (7)).
statement.algorithm_linkage: The result is linked specifically to Algorithm 2, CGS-P, not standard CGS-S. Algorithm 2 computes s_k = Q_(k-1)^T a_k and v_k = a_k-Q_(k-1)s_k, then computes the norm values psi_k = ||a_k||_2 and phi_k = ||s_k||_2 and evaluates the diagonal as sqrt(psi_k-phi_k)*sqrt(psi_k+phi_k) before setting q_k = v_k/r_kk and assembling the partial factors. The paper explicitly contrasts this with Algorithm 1's r_kk = ||v_k||_2 and says the change is necessary for the stated type of result (PDF p. 2, printed p. 300, anchor: paragraph introducing Algorithm 2; PDF p. 3, printed p. 301, anchor: Algorithm 2).
numerical_model: The stated model is IEEE floating-point arithmetic with fl(x+y) = (x+y)(1+delta), |delta| <= epsilon_M, for results in the normalized range (PDF p. 3, printed p. 301, anchor: floating-point model).

The analysis adopts (1+epsilon_M)^(p(n)) = 1+p(n)epsilon_M+O(epsilon_M^2) for a modest function p(n), assuming the quadratic contribution is insignificant (PDF p. 3, printed p. 301, anchor: linear approximation).
Theorem 1 labels Q_k and R_k as computed matrices and compares them with the input submatrix A_k (PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: Theorem 1 and equations (4)-(8)).

In the supporting proof, psi_k and phi_k are explicitly modeled as fl(||a_k||_2) and fl(||s_k||_2), each with relative error bounded by (0.5m+1)epsilon_M+O(epsilon_M^2) (PDF p. 9, printed p. 307, anchor: equations (14)-(15)).

The supporting proof models the computed diagonal as r_kk = sqrt(psi_k-phi_k)*sqrt(psi_k+phi_k)*(1+epsilon_3^(k)), with |epsilon_3^(k)| <= 3epsilon_M+O(epsilon_M^2) (PDF p. 9, printed p. 307, anchor: Lemma 2 proof following equations (14)-(15)).
error_notions: Equation (4) is a normwise factorization residual bound for Q_kR_k-A_k, scaled by ||A_k||_2 (PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: equation (4)).
Equation (5) is a normwise normal-equations or Gram-matrix backward-error bound for R_k^TR_k-A_k^TA_k, scaled by ||A_k||_2^2 (PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: equation (5)).
Equation (6) is a relative perturbation statement comparing the matrix 2-norms of R_k and A_k (PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: equation (6)).
Equation (7) measures loss of column orthogonality by the matrix 2-norm of I_k-Q_k^TQ_k; it is not a componentwise or Frobenius-norm statement (PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: equation (7)).
Equation (8) separately bounds the operator 2-norm of Q_k (PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: equation (8)).
norms: Every norm displayed in Theorem 1 is a subscript-2 norm (PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: equations (4)-(8)).

For matrices, ||.||_2 is the spectral/operator 2-norm, as confirmed by the condition-number definition and the eigenvalue identities relating ||R_k^(-1)||_2 to the smallest eigenvalue of R_k^TR_k; vector occurrences in the algorithms are Euclidean 2-norms (PDF p. 3, printed p. 301, anchor: Algorithm 2; PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: kappa_2 definition and equation (9)).

The selected orthogonality defect is a k x k matrix because Q_k is m x k, so its identity term is I_k even though the paper prints I (PDF p. 3, printed p. 301, anchor: Algorithm 2 block dimensions; PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: equation (7)).
constants_and_indexing: The theorem and its premise apply separately at every index k = 1,...,n, using the first-k-column factors A_k, Q_k, and R_k rather than only the final factors (PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: Theorem 1).
The constants c_1 and c_2 have special k = 1 branches: c_1(m,1) = 1 and c_2(m,1) = m+2 (PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: equation (2)).
For k >= 2, c_1(m,k) = 2*sqrt(2)*m*k+2*sqrt(k), with m*k outside the square root of 2, and c_2(m,k) = 3.5*m*k^2-1.5*m*k+16*k (PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: equation (2)).
The selected coefficient is exactly c_4(m,k) = c_2(m,k)+2c_1(m,k) (PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: equation (2); PDF p. 14, printed p. 312, anchor: final line of the proof of equation (7)).

Both the premise and the selected bound contain the square kappa_2(R_k)^2, not kappa_2(R_k), and use each partial computed R_k rather than the final R_n alone (PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: equations (3) and (7)).
higher_order_terms: The paper explicitly declares a first-order convention in which O(epsilon_M^2) terms make no significant contribution (PDF p. 3, printed p. 301, anchor: linear approximation).

Theorem 1 introduces equations (4)-(8) with the global qualification 'to within terms of O(epsilon_M^2)', although the displayed inequalities themselves omit an explicit remainder (PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: sentence immediately before equations (4)-(8)).

The proof of the selected equation obtains ||I-Q_k^TQ_k||_2 <= c_4(m,k)||R_k||_2^2||R_k^(-1)||_2^2 epsilon_M + O(epsilon_M^2), and the theorem's displayed equation (7) is the corresponding first-order form (PDF p. 14, printed p. 312, anchor: proof of equation (7); PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: equation (7)).

No quantitative constant, sign, or uniformity condition is supplied for the omitted O(epsilon_M^2) remainder in the theorem statement (PDF p. 3, printed p. 301, anchor: first-order convention; PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: Theorem 1).
exceptional_values: The explicitly stated relative-error model is restricted to results in the normalized range (PDF p. 3, printed p. 301, anchor: floating-point model).
If Theorem 1's assumptions fail, phi_k >= psi_k may occur, making the square-root diagonal formula break down and yielding non-real Q and R (PDF p. 7, printed p. 305, anchor: Remark 2).

Within the proof, condition (3) is used to conclude that R is nonsingular and r_kk > 0 for every k; for Algorithm 2 this requires psi_k > phi_k (PDF p. 9, printed p. 307, anchor: Lemma 2 proof following equations (14)-(15)).

The cited passage does not separately specify behavior for overflow, underflow into the subnormal range, NaNs, infinities, division by zero, or a particular IEEE rounding mode beyond the normalized-range relative-error statement (PDF p. 3, printed p. 301, anchor: floating-point model and Algorithm 2).

undebatable_constraints: The theorem concerns the computed factors from Algorithm 2 (CGS-P), whose diagonal is sqrt(psi_k-phi_k)*sqrt(psi_k+phi_k), not Algorithm 1's r_kk = ||v_k||_2 (PDF p. 2, printed p. 300, anchor: paragraph introducing Algorithm 2; PDF p. 3, printed p. 301, anchor: Algorithm 2).
The inherited input is rectangular A in R^(m x n), m >= n, with full column rank n (PDF p. 2, printed p. 300, anchor: standing setup).
Condition (3) is required for every partial factor R_k, and all conclusions are stated for every k = 1,...,n (PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: Theorem 1).

The condition number in both the premise and selected conclusion is kappa_2(R_k) = ||R_k||_2||R_k^(-1)||_2, not kappa_2(A_k) or a condition number of only the final matrix (PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: kappa_2 definition, equations (3) and (7), and Remark 1).

The selected conclusion is exactly the matrix-2-norm loss-of-orthogonality estimate ||I_k-Q_k^TQ_k||_2 <= c_4(m,k)kappa_2(R_k)^2 epsilon_M at first order (PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: equation (7)).

The coefficient is c_4(m,k) = c_2(m,k)+2c_1(m,k), with the piecewise definitions in equation (2), including c_1(m,k) = 2*sqrt(2)*m*k+2*sqrt(k) for k >= 2 (PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: equation (2); PDF p. 14, printed p. 312, anchor: proof of equation (7)).
The exponent on the condition number is two and there is one leading factor epsilon_M (PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: equations (3) and (7)).
Theorem 1 is multi-part: equations (4), (5), (6), (7), and (8) are all conclusions and must be preserved (PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: Theorem 1).

All five displayed conclusions are qualified by the paper's omission of O(epsilon_M^2) terms; equation (7) is not presented as an exact all-orders finite-precision inequality (PDF p. 3, printed p. 301, anchor: first-order convention; PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: sentence before equations (4)-(8); PDF p. 14, printed p. 312, anchor: proof of equation (7)).
The result does not cover an Algorithm 2 run that breaks down because phi_k >= psi_k and produces non-real factors (PDF p. 7, printed p. 305, anchor: Remark 2).

ambiguities.issue: The displayed bounds omit their higher-order remainders, so their status as literal inequalities versus first-order formulas is not self-contained in the displays (PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: Theorem 1, equations (4)-(8)).
ambiguities.evidence: The theorem globally says 'to within terms of O(epsilon_M^2)', while the proof of (7) explicitly ends with a leading c_4 term plus O(epsilon_M^2) before the displayed theorem drops that remainder (PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: sentence before equations (4)-(8); PDF p. 14, printed p. 312, anchor: proof of equation (7)).
ambiguities.impact: A faithful formal contract must either remain explicitly first-order or introduce and bound a remainder; the source does not justify reading equation (7) as a strict all-orders inequality with zero remainder (PDF p. 3, printed p. 301, anchor: first-order convention; PDF p. 14, printed p. 312, anchor: proof of equation (7)).

ambiguities.issue: There is a definitional circularity concerning nonsingularity: kappa_2(R_k) is defined using R_k^(-1), yet the prose says condition (3) assures nonsingularity (PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: kappa_2 definition and paragraph following Theorem 1).
ambiguities.evidence: The proof likewise says 'Using (3), we conclude that R is nonsingular,' although expression (3) already contains ||R_k^(-1)||_2 (PDF p. 9, printed p. 307, anchor: Lemma 2 proof following equations (14)-(15); PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: equation (3)).
ambiguities.impact: A formalization must either assume every R_k is invertible so that condition (3) is meaningful, or define an extended condition number and prove finiteness; the paper does not disambiguate these formulations (PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: equation (3) and nonsingularity prose).

ambiguities.issue: The identity matrix in equation (7) is printed only as I, without an explicit dimension (PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: equation (7)).
ambiguities.evidence: Algorithm 2 constructs Q_k with k columns, so Q_k^TQ_k is k x k; the only dimensionally consistent identity is I_k (PDF p. 3, printed p. 301, anchor: Algorithm 2 block construction; PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: equation (7)).
ambiguities.impact: The contract uses I_k as a dimensionally forced inference, but that subscript is not literally printed in the selected equation (PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: equation (7)).

ambiguities.issue: The paper does not provide a complete operation-by-operation IEEE semantics for Algorithm 2 (PDF p. 3, printed p. 301, anchor: Algorithm 2 and floating-point model).
ambiguities.evidence: It explicitly states only a normalized-range relative-error formula for fl(x+y), while Algorithm 2 also uses inner products, norms, subtraction, square roots, multiplication, and division; later proof bounds summarize some of these operations without naming a precision or rounding mode (PDF p. 3, printed p. 301, anchor: Algorithm 2 and floating-point model; PDF p. 9, printed p. 307, anchor: equations (14)-(15) and computed r_kk bound).
ambiguities.impact: One cannot silently strengthen the source to a fully specified IEEE format, rounding mode, subnormal policy, or exceptional-value semantics beyond the stated normalized-range first-order model (PDF p. 3, printed p. 301, anchor: floating-point model).

ambiguities.issue: The proof line used to derive equation (6) appears to omit epsilon_M inside a square root (PDF p. 14, printed p. 312, anchor: derivation of equation (6)).
ambiguities.evidence: After deriving a factor 1+c_2(m,k)epsilon_M+O(epsilon_M^2), the printed line reads 1+c_3(m,k)epsilon_M+O(epsilon_M^2) = sqrt(1+c_2(m,k)), while the theorem separately defines c_3 = 0.5c_2 and states equation (6) at first order (PDF p. 14, printed p. 312, anchor: derivation of equation (6); PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: equation (2) and equation (6)).
ambiguities.impact: The literal proof line conflicts with its immediately preceding epsilon_M-dependent expression; the explicit theorem definition c_3 = 0.5c_2 remains clear, but repairing the square-root argument to include epsilon_M is an inference rather than literal transcription (PDF p. 14, printed p. 312, anchor: derivation of equation (6)).

contract_plain_english: Start with the paper's standing full-column-rank matrix A in R^(m x n), m >= n, and form the partial computed factors Q_k and R_k using Algorithm 2, CGS-P, with its pythagorean/Cholesky-like diagonal rather than standard CGS's ||v_k||_2 diagonal (PDF p. 2, printed p. 300, anchor: standing setup and introduction of Algorithm 2; PDF p. 3, printed p. 301, anchor: Algorithm 2). Assume for every k that c_4(m,k)epsilon_M kappa_2(R_k)^2 < 1 (PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: equation (3)). Then, for every k, the theorem gives the factorization residual bound (4), the normal-equations residual bound (5), the norm comparison (6), the selected loss-of-orthogonality bound ||I_k-Q_k^TQ_k||_2 <= c_4(m,k)kappa_2(R_k)^2 epsilon_M in (7), and ||Q_k||_2 <= sqrt(2) in (8) (PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: Theorem 1, equations (4)-(8)). All of these are first-order statements made after neglecting O(epsilon_M^2), and the proof of (7) explicitly contains that omitted remainder (PDF p. 3, printed p. 301, anchor: first-order convention; PDF p. 14, printed p. 312, anchor: proof of equation (7)). The result is not a claim about standard Algorithm 1 and does not cover a CGS-P breakdown with phi_k >= psi_k and non-real factors (PDF p. 2, printed p. 300, anchor: distinction from Algorithm 1; PDF p. 7, printed p. 305, anchor: Remark 2).
